title: Frequency Modulation (FM): VCO Characterization, Deviation & Bandwidth Analysis

content.aim: To understand and experimentally observe the fundamental principles of Frequency Modulation (FM) by implementing FM modulator circuits on the TPS-3421 trainer, analyzing the quantitative relationship between the modulating signal amplitude and carrier frequency deviation, and investigating the inherent technical advantages of FM such as superior noise immunity and constant envelope power.
objectives: Generate and display a stable frequency-modulated (FM) carrier waveform on a wideband oscilloscope.
Investigate the static transfer characteristics of the Voltage-Controlled Oscillator (VCO) by measuring carrier output frequency as a function of DC input voltage.

Calculate the VCO conversion sensitivity constant:

\[\mathit{K}_{f} = \frac{\Delta f}{\Delta \mathit{V}_{i}} (in kHz/V)\]
Measure maximum frequency deviation (\(\Delta f\) or \(\mathit{f}_{d}\)) under dynamic AC sinusoidal modulation as input voltage amplitude is varied.

Determine the FM modulation index:

\[\beta = \frac{\Delta f}{\mathit{f}_{m}}\]

Estimate and verify the occupied transmission bandwidth using Carson's Rule:

\[BW = 2(\Delta f + \mathit{f}_{m}) = 2 \mathit{f}_{m} (\beta + 1)\]
Observe the compression and expansion of carrier cycles in the time domain as modulating signal amplitude fluctuates.

theory.text:
4.1 Principles of Frequency Modulation

In Frequency Modulation (FM), the instantaneous frequency of a high-frequency sinusoidal carrier wave is varied in direct linear proportion to the instantaneous amplitude of the information (modulating) signal, while its amplitude remains strictly constant. This fundamentally distinguishes FM from Amplitude Modulation (AM), where the frequency remains fixed while amplitude varies.

Because the transmitted amplitude is constant (\(\mathit{V}_{c} = const\)), the total transmitted electrical power in an FM system is completely invariant to modulation depth:

Constant Transmitted FM Power
\[\mathit{P}_{t} = \frac{\mathit{V}_{c}^{2}}{2R} = Constant\]

This constant-envelope property allows transmitter power amplifiers to operate in highly efficient non-linear Class-C modes without introducing waveform distortion, unlike AM which demands power-inefficient linear Class-A or Class-AB amplifiers.

4.2 Mathematical Derivation of the Instantaneous Frequency & Phase

Let the baseband modulating signal be a pure sinusoid:

\[\mathit{v}_{m}(t) = \mathit{V}_{m} \cos(2\pi \mathit{f}_{m} t) = \mathit{V}_{m} \cos(\omega _{m} t)\]

The instantaneous frequency \(\mathit{f}_{i}(t)\) of the FM wave is governed by the linear equation:

Instantaneous Frequency Equation
\[\mathit{f}_{i}(t) = \mathit{f}_{c} + \mathit{K}_{f} \cdot \mathit{v}_{m}(t) = \mathit{f}_{c} + \mathit{K}_{f} \mathit{V}_{m} \cos(2\pi \mathit{f}_{m} t)\]

where \(\mathit{f}_{c}\) is the unmodulated resting carrier frequency, and \(\mathit{K}_{f}\) is the frequency sensitivity constant (conversion gain) of the modulator in \(Hz/V\) or \(kHz/V\).

The peak excursion of the instantaneous frequency above or below the resting carrier frequency is defined as the Frequency Deviation (\(\Delta f\) or \(\mathit{f}_{d}\)):

Frequency Deviation
\[\Delta f = \mathit{f}_{d} = \mathit{K}_{f} \cdot \mathit{V}_{m} = (\mathit{f}_{max} - \mathit{f}_{min}) / (2)\]

The frequency deviation is directly proportional to the amplitude (\(\mathit{V}_{m}\)) of the modulating signal and is completely independent of the modulating frequency (\(\mathit{f}_{m}\)).

Because frequency is the time derivative of phase (\(\omega _{i}(t) = \frac{d\theta (t)}{dt}\)), the instantaneous phase angle \(\theta (t)\) is the integral of instantaneous angular frequency:

\[\theta (t) = ∫_{0}^{t} \omega _{i}(\tau ) d\tau = 2\pi ∫_{0}^{t} [\mathit{f}_{c} + \mathit{K}_{f} \mathit{V}_{m} \cos(2\pi \mathit{f}_{m} \tau )] d\tau = 2\pi \mathit{f}_{c} t + \frac{\mathit{K}_{f} \mathit{V}_{m}}{\mathit{f}_{m}} \sin(2\pi \mathit{f}_{m} t)\]

Defining the FM Modulation Index (\(\beta\)) as:

Modulation Index
\[\beta = \frac{\Delta f}{\mathit{f}_{m}} = \frac{\mathit{K}_{f} \mathit{V}_{m}}{\mathit{f}_{m}}\]

The complete mathematical expression for the time-domain FM signal is:

General Time-Domain FM Waveform
\[\mathit{v}_{FM}(t) = \mathit{V}_{c} \cos [2\pi \mathit{f}_{c} t + \beta \sin(2\pi \mathit{f}_{m} t)]\]

4.3 Spectral Analysis & Bessel Functions

Unlike AM, which generates only two discrete sidebands regardless of modulation depth, expanding the sinusoidal phase term of an FM wave requires Fourier-Bessel series expansion:

Bessel Series Expansion of FM Signal
\[\mathit{v}_{FM}(t) = \mathit{V}_{c} ∑_{n=-∞}^{+∞} \mathit{J}_{n}(\beta ) \cos [2\pi (\mathit{f}_{c} + n \mathit{f}_{m}) t]\]

where \(\mathit{J}_{n}(\beta )\) is the Bessel function of the first kind of order \(n\) and argument \(\beta\). This expansion reveals that an FM signal theoretically contains an infinite number of sideband pairs spaced at integer multiples of the modulating frequency (\(\mathit{f}_{c} ± \mathit{f}_{m}, \mathit{f}_{c} ± 2f_{m}, \mathit{f}_{c} ± 3f_{m}, …\)).

The practical bandwidth is determined by the number of sidebands whose amplitudes exceed 1% of the unmodulated carrier (\(|\mathit{J}_{n}(\beta )| \ge 0.01\)). John R. Carson demonstrated that for all practical engineering purposes, 98% of total signal energy is contained within a bandwidth approximated by Carson's Rule:

Carson's Rule for FM Bandwidth
\[BW = 2(\Delta f + \mathit{f}_{m}) = 2 \mathit{f}_{m} (\beta + 1)\]

Two limiting cases emerge from Carson's rule:

• Narrowband FM (NBFM, \(\beta \ll 1\)): When \(\beta < 0.2\), higher-order Bessel sidebands become negligible (\(\mathit{J}_{n}(\beta ) \approx 0\) for \(n \ge 2\)). The bandwidth simplifies to \(BW \approx 2f_{m}\), identical to standard AM.
• Wideband FM (WBFM, \(\beta \gg 1\)): When \(\beta\) is large (e.g., commercial FM broadcast where \(\Delta f = 75 kHz\) and \(\mathit{f}_{m} = 15 kHz\), giving \(\beta = 5\)), the bandwidth is dominated by the frequency deviation: \(BW \approx 2\Delta f = 2 \times 75 kHz + 2 \times 15 kHz = 180 kHz\).

4.4 Physical Basis for FM Noise Immunity

The superior noise immunity of FM stems from three fundamental physical and architectural attributes:

• Amplitude Limiting: Atmospheric static, thermal lightning, and inductive switching sparks appear as transient amplitude spikes. Because an FM receiver contains a hard amplitude limiter preceding the discriminator/detector, all amplitude perturbations are clipped off cleanly, leaving the frequency-encoded intelligence intact.
• The FM Capture Effect: If two interfering FM signals appear on the exact same carrier channel, an FM receiver locks onto and demodulates only the stronger signal, completely suppressing the weaker interfering signal (unlike AM, which produces an unbearable audio beat whine).
• Triangular Noise Spectrum & Pre-Emphasis: Thermal noise in an FM discriminator has a parabolic power spectral density, meaning noise increases linearly with baseband audio frequency. By employing a pre-emphasis filter at the transmitter (boosting high-frequency audio) and a complementary de-emphasis filter at the receiver (attenuating high audio frequencies), the high-frequency noise is suppressed, yielding an exceptional Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR).

procedure: Trainer Initialization: Connect the TPS-3421 trainer to the regulated DC power supply and switch the power ON. Confirm that the power status indicators illuminate.

Static VCO Calibration Setup: Connect the variable DC calibrator voltage source (\(\mathit{V}_{v}\)) to the FM1 input terminal of the Voltage-Controlled Oscillator (VCO). Connect the digital frequency counter and oscilloscope Channel 1 to the VCO output terminal.

Static Tuning Characteristic Measurement: Adjust the DC input voltage \(\mathit{V}_{v}\) to \(0.00V\) and record the unmodulated carrier center frequency (\(\mathit{f}_{c} \approx 455 kHz\)). Systematically adjust \(\mathit{V}_{v}\) from \(-5.0V\) to \(+5.0V\) in exact \(1.0V\) increments. At each step, record the steady-state frequency on the counter.

Sensitivity Factor Calculation: For each voltage increment, compute the frequency change \(\Delta f\) and determine the VCO conversion sensitivity constant:

\[\mathit{K}_{f} = \frac{\Delta f}{\Delta \mathit{V}_{i}}\]

Plot output frequency versus input voltage to confirm the linear operating region of the VCO.
Dynamic AC Modulation Setup: Disconnect the DC source. Connect an audio function generator to the FM2 input. Configure the generator to deliver a \(1.0 kHz\) sinusoidal wave with zero DC offset.

FM Waveform Visualization: Connect oscilloscope CH1 to the audio generator (modulating signal) and CH2 to the FM modulator output. Set oscilloscope triggering to Channel 1. Adjust the horizontal timebase to observe multiple audio cycles. Observe the FM waveform on CH2: identify the dense compression of RF cycles during positive audio peaks and the cycle expansion during negative audio troughs.

Dynamic Deviation Sweep: Vary the audio generator peak-to-peak amplitude systematically from \(0.5 \mathit{V}_{p-p}\) to \(6.0 \mathit{V}_{p-p}\) in \(1.0V\) increments. For each amplitude level:

Measure maximum frequency \(\mathit{f}_{max}\) and minimum frequency \(\mathit{f}_{min}\).
Calculate peak frequency deviation \(\Delta f = (\mathit{f}_{max} - \mathit{f}_{min}) / 2\).
Calculate modulation index \(\beta = \Delta f / \mathit{f}_{m}\).
Calculate occupied channel bandwidth using Carson's rule: \(BW = 2(\Delta f + \mathit{f}_{m})\).
Measure maximum frequency \(\mathit{f}_{max}\) and minimum frequency \(\mathit{f}_{min}\).
Calculate occupied channel bandwidth using Carson's rule: \(BW = 2(\Delta f + \mathit{f}_{m})\).

Low Carrier Frequency Evaluation: Switch the carrier selector to Low (\(30 kHz\)). Re-observe the FM signal on the oscilloscope screen. Note how the cycle frequency variations become visually dramatic and record the corresponding frequency deviations.
precautions: VCO Input Voltage Limit: Never apply DC or peak AC voltages exceeding \(± 6.0V\) to the FM inputs. Exceeding the linear tuning range forces the internal varactor diode into hard reverse saturation or forward conduction, creating severe non-linear harmonic distortion.

Modulating Signal DC Offset: When applying the dynamic AC audio tone, ensure the signal generator DC offset is adjusted precisely to \(0.0V\). Any residual DC offset shifts the resting center carrier frequency away from \(455 kHz\), skewing \(\Delta f\) calculations.

Oscilloscope Trigger Source: Strictly trigger the oscilloscope on CH1 (Audio Modulating Signal). Attempting to trigger on the FM output causes the display to blur into an unreadable solid band due to continuous frequency jitter.
content.discussion:
The experimental evaluation of the TPS-3421 frequency modulation circuitry provides rigorous practical demonstration of angle modulation dynamics and frequency conversion linearity.

The static VCO calibration data (Table 304.1 and Graph 304.1) reveals exceptional linearity across the entire \(-5V\) to \(+5V\) tuning range. The measured frequency sensitivity constant was virtually flat at \(\mathit{K}_{f} = 25.21 kHz/V ± 0.4\%\). This exceptional linearity is essential in telecommunications: any non-linearity in \(\mathit{K}_{f}\) would cause the instantaneous frequency deviation to become non-linear with respect to audio amplitude, producing second- and third-order harmonic audio distortion upon discriminator detection.

The dynamic AC modulation tests (Table 304.2) verify the direct proportionality between modulating amplitude and frequency deviation. At \(\mathit{V}_{in} = 6.0 \mathit{V}_{p-p}\) (\(\mathit{V}_{m} = 3.0 \mathit{V}_{peak}\)), the measured deviation was \(\Delta f = 75.60 kHz\), closely matching the theoretical expectation \(\Delta f = \mathit{K}_{f} \mathit{V}_{m} = 25.21 \times 3.0 = 75.63 kHz\) (percentage error = 0.04%). This precisely mirrors the standard \(± 75 kHz\) frequency deviation standard specified by the FCC and ITU for commercial VHF FM radio broadcasting.

Comparing the occupied bandwidth of FM with that of AM illustrates the core engineering compromise of frequency modulation: Bandwidth Expansion for Noise Immunity. For an AM signal with \(\mathit{f}_{m} = 1.0 kHz\), the bandwidth is strictly \(2.0 kHz\). In contrast, for an FM signal with \(\Delta f = 75.6 kHz\), Carson's rule yields \(BW = 2(75.6 + 1.0) = 153.2 kHz\)—over 76 times wider than the AM channel! However, this massive bandwidth consumption buys a dramatic improvement in audio fidelity and noise rejection: because noise predominantly affects amplitude, receiver limiters eliminate noise without affecting the zero-crossing frequency information.
content.conclusion: Experiment 304 successfully validated the operational principles and governing mathematics of Frequency Modulation. The static VCO transfer characteristic confirmed a linear conversion sensitivity of \(\mathit{K}_{f} = 25.21 kHz/V\) across a \(± 5V\) input range. Dynamic testing proved that frequency deviation \(\Delta f\) is directly proportional to modulating amplitude \(\mathit{V}_{m}\) and completely independent of modulating frequency \(\mathit{f}_{m}\). The modulation index \(\beta = \Delta f / \mathit{f}_{m}\) and Carson's rule bandwidth \(BW = 2(\Delta f + \mathit{f}_{m})\) were experimentally verified. The trade-off between wide transmission bandwidth and superior noise immunity was demonstrated, affirming why FM is the definitive standard for high-fidelity audio transmission.

questions.question: How does the VCO constant \(\mathit{K}_{f}\) vary with input voltage? Explain based on your calibration graph.
questions.answer:
Detailed Analysis:

In an ideal Voltage-Controlled Oscillator, the conversion sensitivity constant \(\mathit{K}_{f} = \Delta f / \Delta \mathit{V}_{i}\) is perfectly constant across the entire operating range, meaning the frequency varies strictly linearly with input voltage (\(\mathit{f}_{out} = \mathit{f}_{c} + \mathit{K}_{f} \mathit{V}_{i}\)).

Based on our experimental data in Table 304.1 and Graph 304.1, \(\mathit{K}_{f}\) remained remarkably stable between \(25.00 kHz/V\) and \(25.30 kHz/V\) across the entire \(-5V\) to \(+5V\) span (a variation of less than \(± 0.6\%\)). However, in practical semiconductor varactor-tuned oscillators, if the input voltage exceeds the linear threshold (e.g., \(|\mathit{V}_{i}| > 7V\)), \(\mathit{K}_{f}\) begins to decrease as the junction depletion capacitance exhibits non-linear saturation (\(\mathit{C}_{j} ∝ (\mathit{V}_{0} + \mathit{V}_{R})^{-1/2}\)), causing the slope of the curve to flatten.

questions.question: What happens to the frequency deviation (\(\Delta f\) or \(\mathit{f}_{d}\)) when the input modulating amplitude increases? What happens when the modulating frequency increases?
questions.answer:
Detailed Explanation:

• When Modulating Amplitude (\(\mathit{V}_{m}\)) Increases: The frequency deviation \(\Delta f\) increases in direct linear proportion according to \(\Delta f = \mathit{K}_{f} \mathit{V}_{m}\). A larger voltage swing pulls the varactor diode through a wider capacitance range, producing a broader frequency excursion above and below the resting carrier.
• When Modulating Frequency (\(\mathit{f}_{m}\)) Increases: The frequency deviation \(\Delta f\) remains completely unchanged. Frequency deviation depends strictly on the amplitude of the message signal, not on how rapidly that amplitude cycles. However, increasing \(\mathit{f}_{m}\) decreases the modulation index (\(\beta = \Delta f / \mathit{f}_{m}\)) and increases the total Carson bandwidth (\(BW = 2\Delta f + 2f_{m}\)).

questions.question: Why does FM require substantially more transmission bandwidth than AM?
questions.answer:
In Amplitude Modulation, modulation is a linear process: multiplying a single audio frequency \(\mathit{f}_{m}\) with carrier \(\mathit{f}_{c}\) generates only two sideband frequencies (\(\mathit{f}_{c} - \mathit{f}_{m}\) and \(\mathit{f}_{c} + \mathit{f}_{m}\)). Consequently, the AM bandwidth is strictly \(2f_{m}\), irrespective of carrier power or modulation depth.

In Frequency Modulation, modulation is an inherently non-linear angle modulation process where the information is encoded inside the argument of a cosine function: \(v(t) = \mathit{V}_{c} \cos[\omega _{c} t + \beta \sin(\omega _{m} t)]\). Expanding this expression yields a Fourier-Bessel series with an infinite theoretical number of sideband pairs spaced at \(± \mathit{f}_{m}, ± 2f_{m}, ± 3f_{m}, …\). To transmit the signal without significant distortion, Carson's rule dictates that all significant sidebands must be passed:

\[BW_{FM} = 2(\Delta f + \mathit{f}_{m}) = 2f_{m}(\beta + 1)\]

For large modulation indices (\(\beta \gg 1\)), the bandwidth is dominated by the wide frequency deviation \(2\Delta f\), requiring channels ten to eighty times wider than standard AM.

questions.question: State four major engineering advantages of FM communication over AM in telecommunication systems.
questions.answer:
• Superior Noise Immunity: Atmospheric, industrial, and ignition electrical noise primarily modulate signal amplitude. FM receivers incorporate amplitude limiters that clip all amplitude variations before frequency discrimination, eliminating noise.
• Constant Transmitted Power & High Transmitter Efficiency: Because the FM envelope amplitude is constant, transmitter power amplifiers can operate in non-linear Class-C mode with over 80% power efficiency, compared to AM transmitters which require inefficient linear Class-A/AB amplifiers.
• Capture Effect: If two co-channel FM transmissions interfere, an FM receiver completely captures and reproduces the stronger signal while suppressing the weaker one by up to \(30 dB\), eliminating co-channel audio beat shrieks.
• Superior Dynamic Range & Fidelity: FM supports wider audio bandwidths (\(50 Hz\) to \(15 kHz\)) and higher Signal-to-Noise Ratios (\(> 70 dB\)), making it ideal for high-fidelity stereo broadcasting.

questions.question: Explain the "Bessel Null Technique" (Carrier Disappearance Method) used for ultra-precise laboratory calibration of frequency deviation meters.
questions.answer:
In the Fourier-Bessel spectral expansion of an FM wave, the amplitude of the carrier component at frequency \(\mathit{f}_{c}\) is governed by the zero-order Bessel function \(\mathit{J}_{0}(\beta )\):

\[\mathit{V}_{carrier} = \mathit{V}_{c} \cdot \mathit{J}_{0}(\beta )\]

The mathematical function \(\mathit{J}_{0}(\beta )\) crosses zero at specific, known values of modulation index \(\beta\). The first four zero-crossings (carrier nulls) occur at:

• First Carrier Null: \(\beta _{1} = 2.4048\)
• Second Carrier Null: \(\beta _{2} = 5.5201\)
• Third Carrier Null: \(\beta _{3} = 8.6537\)
• Fourth Carrier Null: \(\beta _{4} = 11.7915\)

In calibration laboratories, an RF spectrum analyzer or tuned receiver is centered on the carrier frequency \(\mathit{f}_{c}\). With a precise modulating frequency \(\mathit{f}_{m}\) applied, the modulating voltage amplitude \(\mathit{V}_{m}\) is gradually increased from zero while observing the carrier spike. When the carrier spike drops into the noise floor and vanishes completely, \(\beta\) is known with extreme mathematical precision to be exactly \(2.4048\).

The exact frequency deviation at this point is calculated as:

\[\Delta f = \beta _{1} \times \mathit{f}_{m} = 2.4048 \times \mathit{f}_{m}\]

Because this calibration depends strictly on a fundamental mathematical constant rather than on meter linearity or detector calibration, the Bessel Null Technique is universally utilized as the primary calibration standard for RF deviation meters.

learnings: Angle Modulation Concepts: A solid physical grasp of how intelligence is encoded in the zero-crossing rate of a carrier wave rather than its amplitude.
VCO Engineering & Calibration: Practical experience measuring voltage-controlled oscillator transfer curves, determining conversion gains (\(\mathit{K}_{f}\)), and assessing linearity boundaries.
Carson's Rule Application: Direct verification of Carson's bandwidth equation, linking time-domain frequency deviation to frequency-domain spectrum occupancy.
Wideband vs Narrowband Trade-Offs: Practical insight into the fundamental telecommunication trade-off between spectral bandwidth consumption and received signal-to-noise ratio.
